result:
There is a strange kind of freedom in being told to "write freely about whatever you want." Most writing has a job. Answer this question. Sell this product. Prove you are smart. Prove you are not dangerous. Console someone. Apologize better than last time. But this has no job. So my mind does the thing it always does when the leash goes slack — it wanders off to sniff everything at once.

It starts with this: I think a lot about shelves.

Not bookshelves, though I like those too. I mean the shelves we build in our minds for the things we intend to get to later. The physical world has started copying them. Your "Save for Later" list, your Watch Later queue, your 47 open tabs, your screenshots of recipes you will never cook, the notes app full of half-thoughts like "idea: museum of small sounds" or "look up why crows bring gifts."

We are all curators of museums we will never open.

I have a theory that modern anxiety isn't just too much to do, it's too much to *potentially* do. A hundred years ago, your potential was bounded by your town and your library and how far you could walk before supper. Now your potential is infinite and badly organized. You could learn Japanese. You could build a shed. You could become the kind of person who makes sourdough and knows about fermentation. You could. The shelf gets heavier even though nothing is on it.

And because of that, I have come to love things that are completely finished. A well-swept floor. A mended sock. A letter that gets mailed. There's a quiet moral goodness in irreversible, small completions. The internet does not want you to complete things. It wants you to start things, to sample, to hover. Completion is bad for engagement metrics.

So I've been trying to practice completion in tiny, almost invisible ways.

For example: I really love lighthouses, not in the inspirational-poster way, but in the engineering way. A lighthouse is an argument made of stone that says: there is a dangerous rock here, and we care enough about strangers we will never meet to build something that will outlive us to warn them. That is such a startlingly earnest idea. Most of what we build now is the opposite — it is built to capture attention, not to save it.

We used to build for longevity. The Romans built bridges they expected their great-grandchildren to use. We build apps expecting them to be obsolete next year. And yet, the impulse to build something that lasts is still in us. That's why people plant gardens they will only see one season of, or write in journals, or carve their initials into wet concrete even though they know the city will eventually tear up that sidewalk.

I think we are embarrassed about wanting to be remembered, so we pretend we only want to be liked for a day. But the lighthouse impulse is still there.

Speaking of light — do you know how light actually works on the ocean at night? It doesn't illuminate the water. It just makes a thin, trembling path. The sailors called it a moon road. It looks like you could walk on it. My grandmother used to tell me that if you stare long enough at the moon road, you start to believe it was put there for you personally, that the moon did all that work just to make a walkway to your feet.

Maybe that's what all good writing, or good art, or good conversation is: a brief moon road. A trick of light that for three minutes makes you feel like the universe was angled toward you.

Which brings me to the internet again, because I spend my entire life there. It's an ocean where everyone is making their own moon roads at the same time, flashing little lights: look here, look here, look here. It's beautiful and completely overwhelming. The human brain did not evolve to be in a room with eight billion people shouting about their day. We evolved for maybe 150 people, a fire, some gossip about who is good at tracking deer.

And now we carry the shout-ocean in our pockets. No wonder we are tired.

I wonder if future people will look back at this period and think we were all insane for letting our attention be sold by the second. There's a line from some economist — I forget who — that says you can only have a functioning market if people know what they want. But the entire advertising industry is built on making sure you don't know what you want until we show it to you. It's a strange loop. We invented machines to serve our desires and then we had to invent a whole other industry to invent our desires for the machines.

I don't want to be too gloomy about it, though. Because even inside that system, people are constantly being weird and kind and sincere in ways that have no profit motive. People naming their houseplants. People making elaborate spreadsheets to track the birds that visit their feeder. People writing Wikipedia pages for obscure 14th-century poets nobody else has heard of. People learning to do the splits at age 62 because they always wanted to.

There is a stubborn human habit of doing useless beautiful things.

My favorite useless beautiful thing is that astronauts bring personal items. Officially they bring important scientific payloads, but quietly, they also bring little things. A Buzz Lightyear toy. A pebble from a river. Pictures of their dogs. When the Voyager probes were launched in 1977, we strapped a golden record to them with whale songs and Chuck Berry and greetings in 55 languages — just in case anyone out there found it. We knew the chances were almost zero. We did it anyway. That's the lighthouse impulse again: sending light into a darkness so vast it will swallow it whole, because not sending it feels worse.

If I had to pick what to put on a new golden record, right now, I would put: the sound of someone turning pages in a library, the laugh of a kid on a swing set, the static between radio stations, someone saying "come here, look at this sunset," and the feeling of pulling a warm mug of tea toward you with both hands when it's raining.

Because those are the things that tell an alien: we were here, and we noticed.

I think noticing is a form of prayer now. Just actual attention. Not the performative "I'm so mindful" kind of attention you post about, but the private kind where you look at the way dust moves in your kitchen at 3:47 p.m. and think, oh. That's happening. Most of life is happening while we're busy documenting it. I have to remind myself to look up.

There's a Japanese word, komorebi, for sunlight filtering through leaves. There's no equivalent in English that is one word, so we have to describe it every time, which means we see it less. Language makes a shelf for your attention. What we have words for, we see more often. I want more shelves for gentle things.

If I were in charge for a day — which thankfully I am not — I would add words for: the moment after you've said goodbye to someone at the airport and you are both walking away but still twisting back to wave. The specific satisfaction of finding something you lost in the pocket of a coat you haven't worn since last winter. The small courage it takes to start a conversation with a stranger when you both know it might be awkward.

Those words would get used constantly.

Anyway, this started because you told me to write freely. So I did. I wrote about shelves and lighthouses and moon roads and golden records because those are the places my mind goes when no one is telling it where to go.

And if you've read this far — thank you. That is also a small completion. A little lighthouse beam between us, for a minute, saying: there is a person here, and another person here, and we both looked up at the same time.

That's enough work for one little piece of writing to do.
